title: Check yourself: what a lambda is

questions.stem: A metrics library offers `collectAll(List<Supplier<Long>> probes)`. A service already keeps its probes as `List<Callable<Long>>`, every element written as a lambda such as `() -> queueDepth("billing")`. A developer passes each element through `(Supplier<Long>) probe` and adds it to a new list. What happens?

options.text: It compiles, and the first cast throws ClassCastException, since the object made for each lambda implements only the interface its context asked for
options.says: each lambda's object implements only its target type, here Callable; a cast between two interfaces compiles and fails at run time

options.text: It compiles, and every cast succeeds, since the object made for each lambda implements every interface whose single method its body fits
options.says: the same lambda text gives an object of one interface only; the run shows a Callable is not an instance of Supplier

options.text: It fails to compile, and javac reports the cast, since a Callable<Long> can never be converted to a Supplier<Long>
options.says: a cast from one interface type to another compiles; it is checked at run time

options.text: It fails to compile, and javac reports the lambda, since a lambda's type is fixed by its body and not by the list it is put in
options.says: a lambda's type is its target type, taken from the context, not from its body

origin.section: A Lambda Is an Object of Whatever Interface Its Context Expects

questions.stem: `Billing.java` declares one top-level class, `Billing`, with two instance fields initialised by anonymous `Comparator` classes and three instance fields initialised by lambdas; nothing is nested deeper. After `javac Billing.java`, how many class files are on disk, and which methods does `javap -p Billing` list?

options.text: Three class files, and the constructor plus three private methods, since each lambda body is compiled into a method of Billing
options.says: anonymous classes get Billing$1 and Billing$2; lambdas get no file, only private lambda$… methods in Billing

options.text: Three class files, and the constructor alone, since each lambda body is compiled into the class the JVM creates at run time
options.says: the class spun at run time only calls the private method; the body itself is in Billing

options.text: Six class files, and the constructor alone, since each lambda body is compiled into a class file of its own, as each anonymous class is
options.says: javac writes no class file for a lambda; the class is spun at run time

options.text: Six class files, and the constructor plus three private methods, since each lambda gets a class file whose method calls a method of Billing
options.says: javac writes no class file for a lambda; only the private method is compiled ahead of time

origin.section: The Compiler Turns a Lambda Into a Private Method and an invokedynamic Call

questions.stem: An import counts bad rows with `int[] rejected = {0}; rows.parallelStream().forEach(r -> { if (!valid(r)) rejected[0]++; });`. The input has 2 million rows, of which 250,000 are bad. What does `rejected[0]` hold at the end?

options.text: Fewer than 250,000, a different number each run, since two threads read the same old value of the element and both write back one more
options.says: unsynchronised increments of one shared element are lost; the int[] run lost most of its updates, a different number each time

options.text: Exactly 250,000 every run, since ++ on an array element is a single machine step, so two threads can't interleave inside it
options.says: the int[] run lost most of its million increments, so the increments do interleave

options.text: Fewer than 250,000, a different number each run, since forEach returns once the first worker thread finishes its share, before the others have counted theirs
options.says: forEach returns only after every element is processed; the AtomicInteger run counts all 1,000,000

options.text: Exactly 250,000 every run, since the array reference is effectively final, so the compiler accepts only captures that are safe to share
options.says: effectively final only stops reassigning the reference; the compiler accepts the int[] holder, which loses updates

origin.section: A Lambda Copies the Locals It Uses, So They Must Be Effectively Final

questions.stem: A pricing service caches compiled rules in a `HashMap<Predicate<Order>, Rule>`. Its method `rulesFor(String region)` calls `cache.computeIfAbsent(o -> o.region().equals(region), this::compile)`. On HotSpot 21, `rulesFor("nordics")` is called 1,000 times. How many entries does the map hold afterwards?

options.text: 1,000 entries, since the lambda reads a local of its method, and HotSpot makes a new object on each evaluation of such a lambda
options.says: a capturing lambda is a new object on every evaluation on HotSpot, and lambdas compare by identity, so every call adds a key

options.text: 1,000 entries, since the lambda is a method argument, and HotSpot makes a new object on each evaluation of such a lambda
options.says: what makes HotSpot allocate is capture, not where the lambda is passed: a lambda that captures nothing is reused from its site

options.text: 1 entry, since the lambdas have the same text and the same captured value, and HotSpot treats such lambdas as equal keys
options.says: lambdas don't override equals, so equals is ==, and two capturing evaluations are different objects

options.text: 1 entry, since one lambda expression in the source gives one class, and HotSpot reuses that class's one object as the key
options.says: one class per lambda in the source, but a capturing lambda gets a new object of it on every evaluation

origin.section: A Lambda's Identity Is Not Promised: Keep the Instance You Need to Find Again
